user_request: Build an AI document intelligence platform using AWS. It should allow users to upload PDF documents, extract text using OCR, store documents securely, provide semantic search and question answering using RAG, support user authentication, and expose APIs for integration with other enterprise systems. Prefer reusable open-source solutions where appropriate, but ensure the selected components have suitable licenses and acceptable security/maturity.
normalized_request: An AWS-hosted document intelligence platform enabling PDF upload, OCR-based text extraction, secure storage, semantic search with RAG-based question answering, user authentication, and REST API exposure for enterprise integration.

requirements.description: Users must authenticate securely before accessing the platform
System must accept and store PDF documents securely with access controls
System must extract text from PDF documents using OCR capabilities
System must index extracted text for semantic search and retrieval
System must answer user questions using retrieved document context (RAG pattern)
System must expose REST APIs for third-party enterprise system integration
System must maintain audit logs and security compliance for enterprise requirements
System must provide observability into document processing and query execution

blueprint.solution_summary: The AI document intelligence platform is architected as a modular system combining REUSE, ADAPT, and BUILD decisions. Core components leverage established open-source solutions: Logto for enterprise authentication with multi-tenancy, Smartdoc for OCR-based text extraction, Haystack for RAG orchestration and semantic search, Mayan-EDMS for secure document storage, and Grafana for observability. ChatPDF is adapted for custom text chunking optimization, and Aegis is adapted for compliance-focused audit logging. Custom development focuses on three critical components: PDF upload ingestion service (asynchronous document workflow entry point), workflow orchestration engine (coordinating OCR → chunking → embedding → indexing pipelines), and REST API gateway (domain-specific composition of document intelligence operations). This hybrid approach balances rapid market time via reusable foundations while maintaining flexibility for enterprise-specific integration requirements (REQ-006, REQ-007, REQ-008). The platform runs on AWS infrastructure with document storage in S3, metadata/embeddings in RDS and vector databases, and processing via Lambda/ECS for scalability. Prerequisites: Python3 Amazon Dataset (3.6GB) Anaconda How this project was made? This project has been built using Python3 to help predict the sentiments with the help of Machine Learning and an interactive dashboard to test reviews. To start, I downloaded the dataset and extracted the JSON file. Next, I took out a portion of 7,92,000 reviews equally distributed into chunks of 24000 reviews using pandas. The chunks were then combined into a single CSV file called balanced_reviews.csv. This balanced_reviews.csv served as the base for training my model which was filtered on the basis of review greater than 3 and less than 3. Further, this filtered data was vectorized using TF_IDF vectorizer. After training the model to a 90% accuracy, the reviews were scrapped from Etsy.com in order to test our model. CountVectorizer is a great tool provided by the scikit-learn library in Python. It is used to transform a given text into a vector on the basis of the frequency (count) of each word that occurs in the entire text. This is helpful when we have multiple such texts, and we wish to convert each word in each text into vectors (for using in further text analysis).  CountVectorizer creates a matrix in which each unique word is represented by a column of the matrix, and each text sample from the document is a row in the matrix. The value of each cell is nothing but the count of the word in that particular text sample.  What is TF-IDF Vectorizer? TF-IDF stands for Term Frequency - Inverse Document Frequency and is a statistic that aims to better define how important a word is for a document, while also taking into account the relation to other documents from the same corpus.  This is performed by looking at how many times a word appears into a document while also paying attention to how many times the same word appears in other documents in the corpus.  The rationale behind this is the following:  a word that frequently appears in a document has more relevancy for that document, meaning that there is higher probability that the document is about or in relation to that specific word a word that frequently appears in more documents may prevent us from finding the right document in a collection; the word is relevant either for all documents or for none.
